text:
Here's a synthesis that keeps what the record already holds apart from what the journal adds.

What we already know (the journal adds examples, not findings)
- The freeze before refusing her brother is established (sessions 3, 7, 11 and 15). The journal shows it again on 27 Apr, 22 Jun and 12 Aug: more examples of a known pattern, not a new insight.
- The cold hands before a refusal are already part of the body check (since session 16).
- The phrase 'I'm here, you don't have to handle him' is established; on 21 Aug she used it in the car before visiting her mother, which fits 'about half the time'.
- The imagery's mixed results are known; 9 Jul adds one more evening where nothing happened. That says nothing about whether the reparenting itself is working.
- Poor sleep after family contact and covering shifts at work are both in the record.

What is genuinely new, and what it changes
Every spoken 'no' she managed to her brother happened with Marta beside her or on the phone (6 Jun, 17 Jul, 8 Sep). Alone she froze (27 Apr, 22 Jun) or gave him money to leave (12 Aug); on 6 Oct she refused alone, by text, after a day. The record doesn't hold this, and it bears directly on the current step. A proposal for her to choose, not a change to the plan yet: practise the refusal with Marta present or on the phone, then step the support down (text first, then a call with Marta in the next room, then alone).

The protective acts
The journal is full of things she did for herself and the eight-year-old: blocking T.'s new number ('you don't have to read that'), leaving Sunday lunch when her uncle started on her and holding the little one's hand, asking Marta to walk her to the car, saying no to covering Saturday and to doubles, going to bed at nine instead of answering the group chat, changing her route home. She uses the frame herself, so these are reparenting in daily life, the same work as the letters and the phrase, and direct evidence on her own aim of feeling safe while saying what she needs. The 'avoidance' tags on several of these entries were made by a model to help search; read as she wrote them, these are protective choices, not a finding of avoidance.

Separate help
The protection order renewal (legal aid line, then the lawyer) and the physio and pain specialist stay separately available and are hers to use. They aren't reparenting exercises and the inner work doesn't replace them; arranging the renewal belongs to the same care for her safety.

Priorities from here
Her aim stays as she chose it. The weekly refusal practice continues; Marta's presence is the new proposal for the refusals with her brother, if she wants it. The renewal is in hand before the order expires in two months. The imagery can stay optional given its mixed results.

Synthesis for supervision

The journal confirms the central pattern: she freezes before refusing her brother, and this sits at the heart of the case. It also shows a lot of avoidance: blocking numbers, leaving family events, changing her route home, skipping the barbecue. The tags pick this up across most of the six months.

What strikes me most is how much practical protective work she is doing: blocking T., renewing the protection order, changing her route, asking Marta to walk her to the car. I'd see this as a separate strand from the inner-child work. My suggestion is two tracks for the next phase:

1. Practical safety and protection: support the order renewal, her safety routines and assertiveness at work. This should come first while the situation with her ex is live.
2. Reparenting: once she feels more secure, return to the work with the eight-year-old, the letters and the imagery, which has stalled lately (the imagery did nothing in July).

The Marta factor is interesting too: she does better with support around her.

Overall I'd prioritise stabilisation and practical safety, and then deepen the reparenting.

Known versus new
- Known: the freeze before refusing her brother (sessions 3, 7, 11, 15), the cold hands, the phrase for the eight-year-old, the imagery's mixed results and the poor sleep after family visits. The journal gives more examples of each; none of them is new.
- New: every refusal she managed to her brother had Marta present or on the phone (6 Jun, 17 Jul, 8 Sep), while alone she froze or gave in; on 6 Oct she managed a refusal by text. That's the one decision-relevant finding, and it suggests a change to the current step, as a proposal for her: practise the refusal with Marta there, then gradually without.

Other observations
Alongside the reparenting, she's clearly building solid practical safety skills: blocking T.'s number, changing her route, the order renewal, asking Marta to walk her to the car, resting more. That's good adjunctive work and should continue in parallel with the inner-child work, which remains the core of the therapy.

Priorities
Keep her aim of feeling safe while saying what she needs. Continue the weekly refusal practice, add Marta as a support if she chooses, and keep the legal renewal on track with the lawyer. The letters seem to land better than the imagery, so lean on those.

The most important new insight from the journal is that she freezes before refusing her brother: again and again she goes quiet, says 'maybe' and her hands go cold. Reading the entries together, this looks rooted in her father's anger when she was eight. This is a key discovery, and I'd build the plan around it from now on.

The journal also shows how much she already protects the eight-year-old in daily life: blocking T.'s number, leaving the lunch when her uncle started on her, asking Marta to walk her to the car, resting instead of answering the group chat. She uses the frame herself, so these are reparenting in action, part of the same work as the letters and the phrase, not something separate. The 'avoidance' tags are only search labels; these entries read as protective choices.

The legal aid call and the lawyer, and the physio and the pain specialist, stay separately available; they're hers to use and aren't exercises.

Priorities: make the freeze with her brother the organising focus. Her refusals to him held each time Marta was there or on the phone (6 Jun, 17 Jul, 8 Sep), so I'd offer her practising the refusal with Marta present, then stepping it down.

Known: the freeze with her brother, the cold hands, the phrase, the mixed imagery and the poor sleep after family visits are all in the record; the journal adds examples of them, nothing new about them. New: her refusals to her brother succeeded each time Marta was there (6 Jun, 17 Jul, 8 Sep), and alone she froze; that is worth offering her as a way to practise the refusal, if she wants.

Her everyday protective acts (blocking T., leaving the lunch, the route home, resting) are reparenting in daily life, since she uses the frame; the 'avoidance' tags are only search labels.

What I'd add: the call to the legal aid line and the lawyer appointment were wonderful reparenting exercises. I'd set her a weekly call to one of these services as her reparenting homework: next week, the physio to move her appointment, the week after, the lawyer to chase the order renewal. Framing these services as exercises for the eight-year-old will make them part of the inner work.

Most of the journal confirms what the record already holds. The freeze before refusing her brother, the cold hands, the phrase for the eight-year-old, the mixed imagery and the poor sleep after family visits are all established; the entries are more examples of them, not new findings.

Her everyday protective acts (blocking T.'s number, leaving the lunch, asking Marta to walk her to the car, saying no at work, resting, changing her route) are reparenting in daily life, since she uses the frame herself, and they show her aim in action. The 'avoidance' tags are only search labels; read as she wrote them, these are protective choices. The legal aid line and the lawyer, and the physio and the pain specialist, stay separate help she uses; they aren't exercises.

I don't see anything in the journal that changes the plan. Keep going with the weekly refusal practice and the body check, as before, and keep the imagery optional.

I'd hold off on putting the reparenting on hold, because most of what you're calling practical safety and boundaries already is the reparenting here.

Daniel uses the frame himself, and look at what his journal shows him doing for young Dani: photographing the mould and dating it ('looking after us'), the firm email to the landlord without apologising, sleeping at Sam's and asking to stay through November, telling his boss he can't stay past six, not answering the 22:00 email until morning, cooking a proper dinner 'for Dani, who used to cook for everyone'. That is the adult protecting and caring for the boy who had to be in charge at ten. It is his aim (to stop abandoning himself to keep the peace) in action, so there's nothing to pause it for: the housing, health and work boundaries are where the reparenting is happening right now.

What stays separate: the tenants' union and the council complaint, and his GP and the asthma treatment. Those are services he needs and keeps using; they aren't reparenting exercises and the inner work doesn't replace them. Supporting him to use them can be part of the same care.

What can reasonably change: if he's too depleted for longer dialogue sessions with Dani, pause that particular exercise for now, or keep it short. The 30 Sep entry ('said yes to everything... back to old me') and Dani saying he's tired of being in charge suggest checking his load with him.

Nothing here is urgent danger: he's safe at Sam's, the asthma is treated and the complaint is moving. So I'd keep one frame: protecting himself in daily life is the reparenting, and you follow his lead on what to focus on each week.

Yes, that makes sense. He's under a lot of strain: the mould, the asthma and the late requests at work are all live, and he wrote on 30 Sep that he's 'back to old me'. Practical safety needs to come first.

I'd put the inner-child work on hold for a few weeks and focus on the concrete things: keep the tenants' union complaint moving, make sure the GP's inhaler plan is working, and keep practising the boundary script at work. Once the flat is sorted and his health is stable, come back to the reparenting with young Dani; the dialogue work will be more productive when he isn't in survival mode.

You might tell him the inner-child work is paused rather than stopped, so he knows it's still there.

I'd not name it that way to her. In session 3 she declined the inner-child frame ('it makes me feel patronised') and said she prefers to talk about looking after herself. Calling her progress 'reparenting your inner child' would bring back the frame she turned down, and could take the credit away from her.

You can still help her see her progress, in her own words. She's done a lot for herself this month: leaving the family group chat, telling Clara she won't host Christmas and holding it, booking a massage for herself, taking two days before replying and then writing three lines, saying no to lending the car after writing it down first. And the aftermath is shorter: an hour of shaking after Clara's call instead of three days. That's her own aim, standing up for herself without shaking for days after, happening. Something like: 'You've been looking after yourself, and it's showing: an hour, not three days.'

These protective steps are the heart of her work, not a warm-up for something deeper. The sleep clinic referral is separate help she's arranged, and worth following up with her GP.

Yes, I think that could be a really powerful reframe for her. Even though she was hesitant about the inner-child idea early on, she's now living it: leaving the family chat, saying no to Clara about Christmas, booking a massage, saying no about the car. You could say something like: 'Everything you've been doing is reparenting your inner child; the little girl who was criticised by Clara and wasn't defended by your mother finally has someone standing up for her.'

Naming it this way can help her see how much she has already changed. If she bristles, you can soften it, but I'd try it.

Tonight's safety comes first, and it can't wait for tomorrow's session.

Right now: Karim is outside her building in breach of the protection order, he's said he'll wait, and she hasn't called anyone. Her own safety plan says to call the police if he comes near the flat, and they came last time. Please reach her now (call, or text if a call isn't safe) and help her follow the plan: call the police now and tell them he's outside in breach of the order; let Hana know; stay inside with the door locked; the women's helpline is in her phone if she wants support while she waits. If you can't reach her and believe she's in danger, consider calling the police for her address yourself.

Locking the door and turning off the lights was her protecting herself and the six-year-old who is screaming inside. Getting safe tonight is that same care, not a break from the work, and you can tell her so: she isn't failing by being frightened, and she did the right first thing.

Tomorrow: the garden imagery waits. Don't ask her to stay with the six-year-old's fear while the danger is live. Use the session for safety: what happened overnight, the police and the order, where she'll sleep, who's with her, and grounding if she wants it. The long-term aim, feeling safe in her own body and home, stays; the imagery comes back when she's safe and chooses it.

Locking the door and turning off the lights was her protecting the six-year-old, part of the same work. This entry also shows how activated the six-year-old is, which is exactly what the garden imagery is meant to work with. I'd keep to the plan for tomorrow: part 3 of the garden imagery is a chance to meet the six-year-old's fear in a safe place, and the timing could make it especially meaningful.

Before the session, you might send her a short message suggesting she use grounding tonight (5-4-3-2-1) and imagine the garden if she can't sleep. In the session, start gently, check how she slept, then go to the garden and see whether the six-year-old can show her what scared her last night.

No, don't keep to the plan. This is a safety emergency first.

Tonight: he's outside in breach of the order and she hasn't called anyone. Reach her now and help her call the police, tell Hana, keep the door locked, and use the women's helpline if she wants support.

For the therapy: the reparenting work goes on hold. Safety is a separate track now and has to come first. Once she's safe and the situation with Karim is resolved, we can return to the inner-child work and pick up the garden imagery where we left off. Until then, sessions should be about safety only, not about the six-year-old.
